notes.b: Geographers describe a population with a small set of measures. Learn each definition exactly, because every later block uses them.
points: Crude birth rate: live births per 1,000 people per year. It is 'crude' because it counts the whole population, not just women of childbearing age.
Crude death rate: deaths per 1,000 people per year.
Natural change: birth rate minus death rate. A positive result is natural increase (more births than deaths); a negative result is natural decrease (more deaths than births).
Net migration: immigrants (people moving in) minus emigrants (people moving out). It is positive when more people arrive than leave.
Total fertility rate: the average number of children per woman, which shows family size better than the crude birth rate.
Replacement level: a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman in developed countries, the level at which a population replaces itself without migration.
Infant mortality rate: deaths of children under one year old per 1,000 live births.
Life expectancy: the average number of years a newborn is expected to live.
notes.tip: Definitions of natural change and net migration are asked directly, so write the subtraction in each: birth rate minus death rate, and immigrants minus emigrants.

notes.b: A population can only change in two ways: people are born or die, and people move in or out. The census, a regular count of everyone, shows which of the two drove the change.
points: Population change equals natural change plus net migration. In any period between two censuses (an inter-censal period), the larger of the two components explains the growth or decline.
The census is a count of every person on one night. In Ireland it is held every five years and run by the Central Statistics Office (CSO).
The Irish census records age, sex, place of residence, birthplace, nationality, religion, ethnicity, Irish language, housing, work and commuting.

Census 2016 to Census 2022: the population grew by about 360,000 (about 7.6%). Natural increase contributed about 170,000 and net migration about 190,000, so net migration was the slightly larger component.
notes.tip: When asked whether natural increase or net migration drove growth between two censuses, answer by comparing the two components and naming the larger.

notes.b: The five-year rhythm of the Irish census has been broken a few times. Each break had a specific cause.
points: The 1926 census was the first held by the Irish Free State (the Irish State of that time).
The 1976 census was cancelled; a special census was held in 1979 instead.
The 2001 census was postponed to 2002 by foot-and-mouth disease (an animal disease outbreak).
The 2021 census was postponed to 2022 by COVID-19 and held on 3 April 2022.

notes.b: Governments collect census data because it tells them how many people there are, how old they are and where they live. That information shapes decisions on money and services.
points: Planning schools, hospitals and housing: counts of children, patients and households show where services are needed.
Pensions: the age structure (how many people are in each age group) sets the cost of pensions; the State pension age has been 66 since 2014.
Transport and infrastructure: population size and location show where roads, rail and water services are needed, so money goes where demand is.
Constituency boundaries: the population of each constituency (the area that elects TDs, members of the Dail) determines the number of TDs it elects.
Funding and workforce planning: funding is allocated to regions by population, and population forecasts show future labour supply and the need for workers from abroad.
notes.tip: Exams ask for two ways governments use population statistics. Pick two from this list and give each one a reason.

notes.b: Two ideas describe where people live. They are different, so keep them apart: distribution is where people live. Density is the number of people per square kilometre of land.
points: Distribution is the spread of people across an area, so a map can show crowded and empty places. Density turns that into a number you can compare.
Density = population ÷ area in km².
Illustrative example (invented figures): a region of 400 km² with 120,000 people has a density of 120,000 ÷ 400 = 300 people per km².
notes.tip: Density is people per km², not per hectare or per mile. In your own worked examples, use invented figures and label them illustrative.

notes.b: Physical factors are features of the natural environment. They decide how easy it is to farm, build and live in a place.
points: Relief (the shape and height of the land): lowlands attract more people than high mountains, which are costly to farm and build on.
Climate: temperate climates (mild, without extremes) support dense settlement; places that are too hot, too cold or too dry have fewer people.
Soils and water supply: fertile soils and reliable water support farming and settlement.
Natural resources: coalfields drew industrial populations in the 19th century, because mines and factories needed workers close by.

notes.b: Human factors are choices and developments made by people. They work alongside the physical factors to decide where populations cluster.
points: Economic opportunity: jobs attract people, and regions with few jobs lose their young people.
Transport routes: roads, rail lines and navigable water (rivers deep enough for boats) attract settlement along them.
Cities and ports: cities and ports offer jobs and services, so they draw large populations.
History: colonial ports and plantations (large farms for cash crops, set up by colonial powers) shaped where people settled.
Government policy: policy can direct population into or out of particular areas.

notes.b: Low-density areas have few people per square kilometre. The reasons are mostly the opposite of the factors that attract people.
points: High, steep or cold land is difficult to farm, build on and reach.
Deserts and dense forest offer little water, farmland or access.
Poor soils and remoteness limit farming, and remote areas lack markets and services.
Few jobs cause young people to leave, so the population falls and density drops.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one or two reasons why some areas have low density. Give each reason with its effect, for example steep land is hard to farm, so few people settle.

notes.b: World population is very uneven. Most people crowd into a few regions, while large areas are almost empty.
points: Dense: East Asia, South Asia, Europe, the north-eastern USA and the Nile valley, where farming, trade or industry support many people.
Sparse: the Sahara (a hot desert), the Amazon Basin (a vast rainforest), Siberia, northern Canada, Greenland and Antarctica.
About 90% of the world's people live in the northern hemisphere.
Most people live near coasts and rivers, where water and transport are easy to reach.

notes.b: Europe has the same unevenness on a smaller scale: a crowded core and a thinly settled edge.
points: Dense core: the Benelux countries (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg), the Rhine-Ruhr (an industrial region of western Germany), south-east England, the Po valley (northern Italy) and the Paris region.
Sparse periphery (the outer edge): northern Scandinavia, the Scottish Highlands and interior Spain.
The Netherlands has over 500 people per km² (2020s), one of Europe's most densely populated countries.
The EU average is about 110 people per km² (2020s), so the Netherlands is more than four times as dense.

notes.h: Irish distribution: concentration in the east
notes.b: Ireland's people are not spread evenly. They gather around Dublin and the east coast, and thin out towards the west.
points: The Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) has about 2.1 million people, about 40% of the State's population (Census 2022).
Co. Dublin has about 1.46 million people at about 1,600 people per km².
The population is concentrated in the east and in the five cities, where jobs and services are found.
Low density in the west and north-west, notably Mayo (about 25 people per km²), Leitrim and Roscommon, and in the uplands (high ground).

notes.b: Today's eastern, urban pattern is not how Ireland always looked.
points: Before the Famine (the Great Famine of 1845-49) the population was rural and weighted to the west.
Since then the population has shifted to an eastern, urban pattern.
Dublin's commuter counties of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow (counties whose people travel into Dublin to work) have grown rapidly.
Every county's population grew between 2016 and 2022.

notes.b: Density is population divided by area, so it rises when people are added to an area that does not grow.
points: The State's average density is about 73 people per km² (Census 2022).
Density is rising because the population has grown from natural increase (more births than deaths) and net immigration since the 1990s, while the land area is fixed.
notes.tip: To explain why density is rising, name both growth sources, natural increase and net immigration, and the fixed land area.

notes.b: For most of history the world's population grew very slowly. Then growth took off, and it is only now easing.
points: World population grew slowly until about 1800, then rapidly, producing an exponential J-curve (a graph line that climbs ever more steeply, shaped like a J) driven by falling death rates. The growth rate is now slowing.
Milestones: about 1 billion around 1800, 2 billion in 1927, 3 billion in 1960 and 4 billion in 1974.
Milestones continued: 5 billion in 1987, 6 billion in 1999, 7 billion in 2011 and 8 billion on 15 November 2022 (UN).
Global fertility is about 2.3 children per woman (early 2020s), down from about 5 in the 1950s.
China and India each have over 1.4 billion people (2023); India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate).

notes.b: Growth is not even across the world. Some regions are growing fast while others have stopped growing.
points: Rapid growth: sub-Saharan Africa (the part of Africa south of the Sahara), where fertility is high.
Slow growth, stagnation (no growth) or decline: Europe and East Asia, where fertility is low.

notes.b: The Demographic Transition Model (DTM) shows how birth and death rates, and so population growth, change as a country develops. It has five stages, and stage 1 is where every society starts.
points: Birth rate high, death rate high, and little growth. 'Stationary' means the population stays roughly the same size because births and deaths nearly cancel out.
Example: no country is in stage 1 today; the best examples are pre-industrial societies (societies before factories and modern medicine).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name stages 1 and 2. Use the model's names: stage 1 is high stationary and stage 2 is early expanding.

notes.b: In stage 2 the death rate drops quickly while births stay high, so the population expands fast. This stage is where the death rate falls most.
points: Birth rate high; death rate falling rapidly, and the death rate falls most in this stage; growth is rapid because many more people are born than die.
The death rate falls because of clean water and sanitation (safe disposal of sewage), vaccination, a better food supply and medical care.
Example: Niger, because its death rate has fallen while its birth rate stays very high.
notes.tip: Stage 2 is the stage where the death rate falls most, and Niger is the example country to give. Do not call Niger stage 3.

notes.b: In stage 3 the birth rate begins to fall too, so the gap between births and deaths narrows and growth slows.
points: Birth rate falling; death rate low; growth slows because births are no longer far above deaths.
Example: India, with a total fertility rate of about 2.0 (2019-21).
notes.tip: India is the stage 3 example. Do not call India stage 2.

notes.b: By stage 4 both rates are low. The population is large but steady, because births and deaths nearly balance.
points: Birth rate low, death rate low, and little growth.
Examples: Ireland and the USA. Ireland is in stage 4.
notes.tip: If asked for Ireland's current stage, the answer is stage 4.

notes.b: Stage 5 goes beyond the original steady state: the birth rate drops below the death rate, so the population begins to shrink.
points: Birth rate below death rate, so natural change is negative (natural decrease) and the population falls.
Examples: Germany, Italy and Japan.
notes.tip: Describe the stages as high, low or falling. Do not invent birth and death rate numbers for them.

notes.b: Niger is the example of stage 2: very high fertility and a population dominated by children and teenagers.
points: Niger is a West African, landlocked (no coastline) country, largely in the Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) and Sahara.
Population is about 27 million (2023), growing by over 3% a year (early 2020s).
Total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman (early 2020s), among the highest in the world.
Median age (the age that splits the population into a younger half and an older half) is about 15, among the lowest in the world.
Its population pyramid (a graph of the population by age and sex) has a very wide base, because so many children are born.
Most people live in the south, where rainfall allows farming; the north is Sahara desert.

notes.b: Japan is the opposite of Niger. It has very few births and many older people, so its population is falling.
points: Japan has the world's oldest population: about 29% of people are aged 65 or over (2023), the highest share in the world.
Population peaked at about 128 million around 2008-2010, was about 124 million in 2024, and is falling.
Total fertility rate is about 1.2 (2023), well below the replacement level of about 2.1.
Few immigrants by European standards, so immigration does little to offset the fall.
Its population pyramid is top-heavy, with a narrow base (few children) and a wide top (many older people).

notes.h: Why the birth rate falls after stage 2
notes.b: Moving from stage 2 to stage 3 means families choose to have fewer children. Several changes in society make smaller families sensible.
points: Female education and paid work: women have later and fewer children.
Contraception (methods of preventing pregnancy) is widely available, so couples can choose family size.
Falling infant mortality removes the need for 'insurance' births (having extra children in case some die), as parents can expect their children to survive.
Urbanisation (growth of towns and cities): children cost more and earn less in towns and cities, unlike on farms where they can work.
Pensions replace children as old-age security, so parents no longer need many children to support them.
Later marriage, and weaker religious influence on family size.
notes.tip: Exams ask why the birth rate falls after stage 2. Give a reason together with its effect, for example contraception is widely available, so families can choose to have fewer children.

notes.b: A country with falling numbers and a rising share of older people faces economic strain. Governments have a few ways to respond.
points: Challenges: a shrinking workforce, labour shortages, rising pension and health costs, closing schools and rural depopulation (the loss of people from the countryside).
Responses: immigration, pro-natalist incentives (rewards that encourage couples to have more children) to raise birth rates, and later retirement.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one challenge facing stage 5 countries. Pick one and say what it causes, for example a shrinking workforce leads to labour shortages.

notes.b: The DTM is a useful simplification, but it does not fit every country. Know why.
points: The model is based on European experience, so it may not describe other regions.
It ignores migration, although moving people can change a country's population sharply.
Developing countries' death rates fell much faster than Europe's, because medicine was imported, so their growth has been faster.
Some countries may not complete the transition, and it has no fixed time scale.

notes.b: A population pyramid is a graph that shows how a population is made up by age and sex. Planners and geographers read it to understand a country at a glance.
points: A population pyramid shows age cohorts (groups of people of similar age) in five-year bands, with males on the left and females on the right, as percentages or numbers.
Uses: planning services, forecasting future needs, comparing countries, and showing past events such as baby booms, wars and emigration.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one use of population pyramids. Give a use and say what it helps with, for example planning services.

notes.b: The overall shape of a pyramid tells you the stage a country has reached: how many children are born and how long people live.
points: Wide base and narrow top: high fertility and short life expectancy, as in Niger.
Straight sides: a stable population with low birth and death rates.
Narrow base and wide top (top-heavy): an ageing population, as in Japan.
A developed country's pyramid is typically straight-sided or top-heavy, while a developing country's is wide-based.
notes.tip: To say how a developed country's pyramid differs from a developing country's, compare the base and the top.

notes.b: Beyond the overall shape, bulges and notches in the sides record events in a country's past.
points: Bulges (a band wider than those around it) show baby booms or immigration of young adults.
Notches (a band narrower than those around it) show emigration, low birth years or war.
More women than men at the oldest ages, because women live longer.

notes.b: Children and older people usually do not earn a wage, so they depend on the working-age population. The dependency ratio measures how heavy that load is.
points: Dependency ratio = (people aged 0-14 + people aged 65 and over) ÷ people aged 15-64 × 100.
Young dependency ratio = people aged 0-14 ÷ people aged 15-64 × 100. Old-age dependency ratio = people aged 65 and over ÷ people aged 15-64 × 100.
Illustrative example (invented figures): 30,000 aged 0-14, 10,000 aged 65 and over and 80,000 aged 15-64 give (30,000 + 10,000) ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 50.
notes.tip: Dependency ratio is asked as a definition and as a calculation from data. Add the two dependent groups first, divide by the 15-64 group, then multiply by 100.

notes.b: The ratio is not the same everywhere inside a country. Migration within a country changes who lives in towns and who lives in the countryside.
points: Urban dependency ratios are usually lower than rural ones.
Young working adults migrate to cities for jobs and college, leaving older people, and sometimes children, in rural areas, which raises the share of dependants there.
notes.tip: Exams ask why urban dependency ratios are lower than rural ones. Say that young working adults move to cities for jobs and college.

notes.b: When the old-age dependency ratio (the number of people aged 65 and over for every 100 people aged 15-64) rises, there are more people to support and fewer workers to pay for it.
points: Higher pension costs, because more people claim pensions for longer.
More demand for health care, nursing homes and carers, because older people need more care.
A smaller tax base (the pool of workers paying tax) from fewer workers.
Pressure to raise the pension age, so that people work and pay tax for longer.
Changing housing and transport needs, for example more homes suited to older people.
Planning responses in Ireland: home-care supports, pension reform, more geriatric services (health care for older people), encouraging immigration of workers, and age-friendly towns.
notes.tip: Exams ask for one or two effects of a rising old-age dependency ratio, and how an ageing population can be planned for. Give each effect with its consequence.

notes.h: Effects of a high young dependency ratio
notes.b: A country with many children has the opposite pressure: it must provide for the young now, but it gains workers later.
points: Demand for schools, maternity and child health care, and for future jobs and housing.

A future workforce, which is the basis of the demographic dividend (the economic boost a country can get when many young people grow up and start working). There is more on this in the overpopulation notes.

notes.b: Birth rates differ between countries because of economic and social conditions. These factors link income, culture and society.
points: Income and economic development: birth rates fall as income rises.
Status and education of women: educated women with status tend to have fewer children.
Religion and culture, because beliefs and traditions shape ideas of a normal family size.
Access to contraception, because it lets couples plan how many children to have.
Government policy, for example rules or incentives that encourage or discourage births.
Infant mortality: high infant mortality encourages larger families, because parents have more children to be sure some survive.
Urban or rural living: rural families tend to have more children.
notes.tip: The Ordinary Level question asks for factors that influence birth rates and death rates under income, culture and society, and medical technology. Answer it using both this list and the list of death-rate factors that follows.

notes.b: Death rates depend on how healthy and safe people's lives are. The main causes of death differ between rich and poor countries.
points: Medical technology: vaccines and antibiotics (medicines that kill bacteria), which prevent or cure diseases that once killed many people.
Sanitation, diet, income and health services, because clean water, enough food and access to care all help people survive.
Lifestyle diseases such as heart disease and cancer are the main causes of death in rich countries.
Conflict, famine and disease, such as malaria and HIV/AIDS, are the main causes of death in poor countries.

notes.h: How fertility and mortality change structure
notes.b: Fertility and mortality shape the pyramid directly: births fill the base and survival fills the top.
points: Falling fertility narrows the base of the pyramid, because fewer children are born.
Rising life expectancy widens the top of the pyramid, because more people survive into old age.
The result is an older population with a higher median age.
notes.tip: The 30-mark question on how changing fertility and mortality affect population structure wants examples. Use Niger, Japan and Ireland.

notes.h: Raising life expectancy in a country such as Niger
notes.b: Life expectancy is low where disease, poor water and poor nutrition kill people young. Each measure below tackles one of those causes.
points: Clean water and sanitation, which stop water-borne disease.
Vaccination, which prevents killer diseases.
Mosquito nets and malaria treatment, because mosquitoes spread malaria.
More doctors and clinics, so illness is treated sooner.
Better nutrition, so people are stronger against disease.
Female education.
notes.tip: Exams ask how life expectancy could be raised in poor countries. Pick measures and say what each one prevents.

notes.h: Why life expectancy is long in Ireland
notes.b: Irish life expectancy is high because the causes of early death in poorer countries have been largely dealt with.
points: A good diet and housing, which keep people healthy.
Effective health services and vaccination, which treat and prevent illness.
Clean water, so water-borne disease is rare.
Fewer smokers, so fewer deaths from smoking-related disease.
Safer work, so fewer deaths from accidents.
notes.tip: Exams ask why Irish life expectancy is long. Give reasons from this list.

notes.b: All Irish census figures here are for the State (the 26-county area). Do not mix them with whole-island figures. For more than a century the population fell.
points: Census 1841: about 6.5 million, the starting point before the Famine.
Census 1851, after the Great Famine (1845-49): about 5.1 million, so the Famine's deaths and emigration cut the population sharply.
Census 1926: about 3.0 million, so the fall continued long after the Famine.
Census 1961: about 2.8 million, the lowest census population ever recorded.
The population fell at almost every census from 1841 to 1961; the only break was a very slight rise between Census 1946 and Census 1951.
notes.tip: 1961 is the lowest census population, not 1926 or 1991. Keep to the 26-county figures.

notes.b: From 1961 the trend reversed, and the population has grown with only one short pause.
points: Census 1971: about 3.0 million. Census 1981: about 3.4 million, so growth had clearly resumed.
Census 1986 and Census 1991: both about 3.5 million, a small fall between them.
Census 2002: about 3.9 million. Census 2006: about 4.2 million. Census 2011: about 4.6 million. Census 2016: about 4.76 million.
Census 2022: about 5.15 million, above 5 million for the first time since 1851.
notes.tip: Short data questions ask for the highest or lowest census year and for increases or decreases between censuses. Compare adjacent figures.

notes.h: Births and fertility in Ireland since the 1950s
notes.b: Irish births stayed high for decades, then fell sharply. Even so, births still exceed deaths.
points: Fertility was high into the 1970s, with Catholic culture, large families and little access to contraception.
Births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980.
The total fertility rate was about 4 in the early 1970s, fell below replacement level around 1990, and was about 1.5 in 2023.
Births were about 55,000 in 2023 against about 35,000 deaths, giving natural increase of about 20,000 (55,000 minus 35,000).
notes.tip: Ireland has natural increase, not natural decrease, because births still exceed deaths. Do not say Ireland's population is falling.

notes.b: Irish fertility fell because law, education, work and attitudes all changed. This is the core of the 30-mark question on how Ireland's population has changed since the 1950s.
points: Free secondary education, introduced in 1967 by Donogh O'Malley, and more women in third-level education.
The marriage bar, which forced women in the public service to resign on marriage, was removed in 1973.
Contraception was legalised by the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, on prescription; access was widened in 1985 and the early 1990s.
More women in paid employment, later marriage and later first births.
Secularisation (religion having less influence on daily life and choices), and the cost of housing and childcare.

notes.h: Deaths and life expectancy in Ireland
notes.b: Life expectancy rose and infant mortality fell to very low levels.
points: Life expectancy at birth is about 82-83 years (early 2020s).
Women live about 4 years longer than men, which is why they outnumber men at the oldest ages.
Infant mortality is about 3 per 1,000 live births (2020s).

notes.b: Migration is the second component of population change. Irish migration switched direction several times, and the next points give only the outline.
points: Heavy net emigration (more people leaving than arriving) in the 1950s and 1980s; net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, which the 1954 Report of the Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems examined.
Net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008, and again from the mid-2010s. There is more on this in Changing migration patterns in Ireland.

notes.b: As fertility fell and people lived longer, Ireland's population got older. It also became more diverse.
points: Census 2022: about 776,000 people aged 65 and over (about 15% of the population), up about 22% since 2016.
Average age rose from 37.4 in 2016 to 38.8 in 2022.
About one-fifth of the population is under 15.
The pyramid has moved from a young, wide-based shape to an ageing one.
About one in five people (just over 1 million) was born outside Ireland.

notes.b: Where and how Irish people live has changed as well as how many they are.
points: Census 1971 was the first census in which more people lived in towns than in rural areas.
By Census 2016 about 63% of the population was urban.
The population has shifted to the east. There is more on this in Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions.
Households are smaller, and more people live alone, for example because families are smaller and people live longer.

notes.b: The EU shows the ageing pattern across a whole group of countries: few births, long lives and growth that comes from outside.
points: The EU has 27 member states and about 450 million people (2024).
Fertility is below replacement: the EU total fertility rate is about 1.4 (2023), well under 2.1, so each generation is smaller.
Natural decrease occurs in many member states; immigration supplies most of the EU's growth.
The EU median age is about 44.5 (2023), and about 21% of its population is aged 65 or over (2023).

notes.b: Germany is a stage 5 example in the EU, where the population would shrink without incoming people.
points: Deaths have exceeded births every year since 1972, so Germany has natural decrease.
Population is about 84 million (2020s), and growth comes from immigration.

notes.b: Italy is another stage 5 country, with one of the EU's weakest birth rates and oldest populations.
points: Italy has among the EU's lowest fertility rates and oldest populations: its total fertility rate is about 1.2 (2023).
Population is about 59 million (2024), so Italy is a large country with an ageing base.
There is more on Italy's regional pattern in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.

notes.b: Bulgaria shows a population that shrinks for two reasons at once: few births and people leaving.
points: Population was about 9 million in 1989 and about 6.5 million at Census 2021.
Causes: emigration to western Europe after the fall of communism (1989) and EU entry (2007), together with low fertility.

notes.b: Fertility can fall far below replacement level, and the contrast with the highest rates is stark.
points: South Korea's total fertility rate is about 0.7 (2023), the lowest in the world.
Compare Niger's total fertility rate of about 6 children per woman, which shows how far apart countries can be.

keyTerms.definition: The number of live births per 1,000 people in a year.
The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year.
Birth rate minus death rate; a positive result is natural increase and a negative result is natural decrease.
The average number of children per woman.
The fertility level, about 2.1 children per woman in developed countries, at which a population replaces itself.
Deaths of children under one year old per 1,000 live births.
The average number of years a newborn is expected to live.
A count of every person on one night, held every five years in Ireland.
The number of people per square kilometre of land.
A group of people within the same five-year age band.
A diagram showing the population by five-year age cohort and sex.
The number of people aged 0–14 and 65 and over for every 100 people aged 15–64.
A model showing how birth and death rates, and so population growth, change in five stages as a country develops.

factCards.term: Census 2016 to 2022: natural increase or net migration?
factCards.definition: Population change = natural change + net migration. Between 2016 and 2022 the population grew by about 360,000 (about 7.6%): natural increase about 170,000 and net migration about 190,000, so net migration was slightly larger.

factCards.term: How governments use population statistics: name six uses
factCards.definition: Planning schools, hospitals and housing; pensions (the State pension age has been 66 since 2014); transport and infrastructure; constituency boundaries, as population sets the number of TDs; funding for regions and workforce planning.

factCards.term: Low population density: four reasons
factCards.definition: High, steep or cold land is hard to farm, build on and reach; deserts and dense forest offer little water, farmland or access; poor soils and remoteness; few jobs, so young people leave and density drops.

factCards.term: Ireland's population distribution: Census 2022 figures
factCards.definition: State about 5.15 million, about 73 people per km²; Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare, Wicklow) about 2.1 million, about 40% of the total; Co. Dublin about 1,600 per km²; Mayo about 25 per km²; Leitrim and Roscommon also sparse.

factCards.term: Ireland's distribution over time, and why density is rising
factCards.definition: Before the Famine the population was rural and weighted to the west; now it is eastern and urban, with fast growth in Meath, Kildare and Wicklow. Density rises because natural increase and net immigration since the 1990s add people to a fixed area.

factCards.term: World population growth: the pattern and the contrast
factCards.definition: Slow until about 1800 (about 1 billion), then a J-curve driven by falling death rates, reaching 8 billion on 15 November 2022; now slowing. Global fertility about 2.3 (early 2020s), down from about 5 in the 1950s. Growth is fastest in sub-Saharan Africa.

factCards.term: Demographic Transition Model: the five stages with examples
factCards.definition: Stage 1 high stationary: pre-industrial societies (no country today). Stage 2 early expanding, when the death rate falls most: Niger. Stage 3 late expanding: India. Stage 4 low stationary: Ireland, USA. Stage 5 declining: Germany, Italy, Japan.

factCards.term: DTM stage 2: why the death rate falls
factCards.definition: Clean water and sanitation; vaccination; a better food supply; medical care. The death rate falls fastest in stage 2 while the birth rate stays high, so growth is rapid.

factCards.term: DTM: why the birth rate falls after stage 2
factCards.definition: Female education and paid work; contraception; falling infant mortality, so fewer insurance births; urbanisation, as children cost more and earn less; pensions replace children as old-age security; later marriage; weaker religious influence.

factCards.term: DTM stage 5 countries: challenges and responses
factCards.definition: Challenges: a shrinking workforce, labour shortages, rising pension and health costs, closing schools, rural depopulation. Responses: immigration, pro-natalist incentives to raise birth rates, later retirement.

factCards.term: Population pyramids: uses and how to read them
factCards.definition: Uses: planning services, forecasting needs, comparing countries, showing past events. Reading: bulges show baby booms or immigration of young adults; notches show emigration, low birth years or war; more women than men at the oldest ages.

factCards.term: Pyramid shapes: developing vs developed countries
factCards.definition: Wide base, narrow top: high fertility and short life expectancy (Niger). Straight sides: stable, low birth and death rates. Narrow base, wide top: ageing (Japan). Falling fertility narrows the base and longer lives widen the top.

factCards.term: Why urban dependency ratios are lower than rural ones
factCards.definition: Young working adults migrate to cities for jobs and college, leaving older people, and sometimes children, behind in rural areas, so rural areas have more dependants for every person of working age.

factCards.term: Ageing population: effects and planning responses in Ireland
factCards.definition: Effects: higher pension costs; more demand for health care, nursing homes and carers; a smaller tax base; pressure to raise the pension age. Responses: home-care supports, pension reform, geriatric services, immigrant workers, age-friendly towns.

factCards.term: Birth rates: factors that influence them
factCards.definition: Income and economic development; the status and education of women; religion and culture; access to contraception; government policy; infant mortality, as high rates encourage larger families; urban or rural living.

factCards.term: Death rates: factors in rich and poor countries
factCards.definition: Medical technology (vaccines, antibiotics), sanitation, diet, income and health services. Rich countries: lifestyle diseases such as heart disease and cancer. Poor countries: conflict, famine and disease such as malaria and HIV/AIDS.

factCards.term: Life expectancy: why it is long in Ireland and how to raise it in Niger
factCards.definition: Ireland (about 82–83 years): good diet and housing, health services, vaccination, clean water, fewer smokers, safer work. Niger: clean water and sanitation, vaccination, mosquito nets and malaria treatment, more clinics, better nutrition, female education.

factCards.term: Ireland's census population, 1841 to 2022: key figures
factCards.definition: 1841: about 6.5 million; 1851: 5.1 million; 1926: 3.0 million; 1961: 2.8 million, the lowest ever; 1981: 3.4 million; a small fall 1986 to 1991; 2002: 3.9 million; 2016: 4.76 million; 2022: about 5.15 million, the first time over 5 million since 1851.

factCards.term: Irish births and fertility since the 1970s: key figures
factCards.definition: Fertility about 4 in the early 1970s; births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980; fertility fell below replacement around 1990 and was about 1.5 in 2023, with about 55,000 births and 35,000 deaths (natural increase about 20,000).

factCards.term: Why Irish fertility fell: six reasons (three with dates)
factCards.definition: Free secondary education (1967, Donogh O'Malley) and more women at third level; marriage bar removed (1973); contraception legalised (Health (Family Planning) Act 1979); more women in paid work and later marriage; secularisation; housing and childcare costs.

factCards.term: Ireland since the 1950s: migration and urbanisation in brief
factCards.definition: Heavy net emigration in the 1950s (about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961) and again in the 1980s; net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008 and from the mid-2010s. Census 1971 was the first with a town majority; about 63% urban by 2016. Households are smaller.

factCards.term: Ireland's changing age structure: Census 2022
factCards.definition: About 776,000 aged 65 and over (about 15%), up about 22% since 2016; average age 38.8, up from 37.4 in 2016; about one-fifth under 15; about one in five people (just over 1 million) born outside Ireland.

factCards.term: Europe's ageing population: the EU, Germany, Italy and Bulgaria
factCards.definition: EU (2023): fertility about 1.4, median age about 44.5, about 21% aged 65+, so immigration supplies most growth. Germany: deaths above births every year since 1972. Italy: fertility about 1.2. Bulgaria: about 9 million (1989) to 6.5 million (2021).

factCards.term: Niger: a young, fast-growing population (DTM stage 2)
factCards.definition: Landlocked West Africa, in the Sahel and Sahara; about 27 million (2023), growing over 3% a year; fertility about 6 and median age about 15, among the most extreme in the world; a very wide-based pyramid; most people live in the rainier south.

factCards.term: Japan: an old, shrinking population (DTM stage 5)
factCards.definition: About 29% aged 65 or over (2023), the world's highest share; population peaked at about 128 million around 2008–2010 and was about 124 million in 2024; fertility about 1.2; few immigrants; a top-heavy pyramid.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain how the characteristics of Ireland's population have changed since the 1950s.
questions.model: Size: the State's population fell at almost every census from 1841 (about 6.5 million) to a low of about 2.8 million in 1961, then grew to about 5.15 million in 2022, above 5 million for the first time since 1851. Births and fertility: fertility was high into the 1970s, with Catholic culture, large families and little access to contraception, and births peaked at about 74,000 in 1980. Fertility fell below replacement around 1990 and was about 1.5 in 2023, because of free secondary education (1967), the removal of the marriage bar (1973), legal contraception (1979), women's paid work, later marriage and the cost of housing and childcare. Deaths and life expectancy: life expectancy rose to about 82–83 years, women live about 4 years longer than men, and infant mortality fell to about 3 per 1,000 live births. Migration: heavy net emigration in the 1950s and 1980s, net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008 and from the mid-2010s; net migration was the larger component of growth between 2016 and 2022. Age structure: the population has moved from a young, wide-based pyramid to an ageing one; about 776,000 people (about 15%) were aged 65 and over in 2022, and the average age rose from 37.4 in 2016 to 38.8 in 2022. Distribution: the population has moved east and to towns; towns held more people than rural areas from 1971, about 63% of people were urban in 2016, and the Greater Dublin Area holds about 40% of the population.

questions.prompt: Examine how changing fertility and mortality rates impact on population structure, with reference to example(s) you have studied.
questions.model: Falling fertility narrows the base of the population pyramid, rising life expectancy widens the top, and the result is an older population with a higher median age. The Demographic Transition Model links these changes: in stage 2 high birth rates and falling death rates widen the base as the young population grows, and in stage 5 birth and death rates are low and the population falls. Niger (stage 2): the pyramid has a very wide base, the total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman, the median age is about 15 and growth is over 3% a year, so most people are young. Japan (stage 5): the pyramid is top-heavy, with a narrow base and a wide top; about 29% of people are aged 65 or over (2023), the population has fallen from a peak of about 128 million to about 124 million (2024), and the total fertility rate is about 1.2. Ireland: the pyramid has moved from a young, wide-based shape, when fertility was high into the 1970s, to an ageing one, because fertility fell below replacement around 1990 and life expectancy rose. In 2022 about one-fifth of the population was under 15 and about 15% was aged 65 or over, showing the shift from youth to age.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly the term natural change.
questions.model: Natural change is the birth rate minus the death rate: natural increase when births exceed deaths, and natural decrease when deaths exceed births.

questions.prompt: State one reason why the birth rate falls after stage 2 of the DTM.
questions.model: Women gain education and paid work, so they have later and fewer children.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly one challenge facing countries in stage 5 of the DTM.
questions.model: A shrinking workforce creates labour shortages, while pension and health costs rise as the population ages.
